Chapter 2. The First Murder and the Power of Myth.
Imagine a time before cities, before nations—even before written language. Picture people gathered around a fire, sharing stories that tried to make sense of the world. Some of those stories explained where everything began. Others warned about dangers hidden in the human heart.
One of the oldest stories is about two brothers—each hoping to win favor with their offerings. One brings his finest sheep. The other, the fruits of his hard work. But when only one gift is accepted, jealousy creeps in. That’s when the world witnesses its very first murder.
The story of Cain and Abel is more than just a warning. It’s like a mirror, showing us the struggles that shape our closest relationships—envy, rejection, and the longing to be accepted. People have wondered for generations: why was Cain’s offering turned away? Was it something about the gift itself, or maybe the attitude behind it? The story doesn’t give a clear answer, and that mystery leaves room for countless interpretations. That’s exactly how myth takes root and grows.
Even today, we wrestle with the same feelings that haunted Cain. Think about a worker passed over for a promotion, a kid trying so hard for a parent’s praise, or a friend who’s left out of a big celebration. Those moments—small stings and silent hurts—echo the ancient story. Most of us don’t act on those feelings, but let’s be honest: the urge to lash out, to make someone else pay for our pain, is something almost everyone knows.
Here’s something easy to miss: the story of Cain and Abel hasn’t just shaped religious ideas. It’s woven into the very symbols we use to talk about good and evil. There’s the mark placed on Cain—meant to protect him from revenge. It ends up symbolizing both punishment and mercy. Over time, artists and writers have reimagined this mark. Sometimes it’s a literal scar, other times a powerful metaphor for guilt, survival, or being set apart.
In comics and pop culture, these ancient symbols get a whole new life. The idea of someone marked by tragedy—set apart from everyone else—becomes the foundation for so many heroes and villains. The line between sinner and savior gets blurry. Suddenly, the stories we tell about ourselves matter just as much as the facts of our lives.
As the tale of Cain and Abel moves through history, it’s clear: myths aren’t just old stories. They’re living frameworks, shaping how we see ourselves and each other. The real power of myth is in its ability to adapt, to find fresh meaning as the world changes. Sometimes, the truths that matter most are hidden inside stories we think we already know.
